title: Packaging Development
html:
“I have a product idea, but no package.”

That is a perfectly good place to begin.

Packaging development does not begin by immediately choosing a pouch, bag, bottle, box, film or foil. It begins with your product, the customer who may buy it, and the marketplace where the product must compete.

We first talk about what the product is, how it will be used, where it will be sold and what packaging customers already recognize in that market.

Explore the starting points:

  • Your Product
  • Your Customer and Marketplace
  • Wholesale Distribution
  • Retail Shelves
  • Online e-Commerce
  • All of the Above
  • Current Marketplace Packaging
  • Package Size and Product Use

These answers help us work from the marketplace backward. They begin defining the package without forcing the project into a structure too early.

Once we understand the product and customer, the next conversation is about protection: what must remain inside the package and what must stay outside.

  • Continue to Product Protection & Barrier Requirements
  • Begin a Project Review

title: Product Protection & Barrier Requirements
html:
What does your product need from its package?

A package may look attractive and still fail if it does not protect product quality, flavor, aroma, freshness or expected shelf life.

This is where we discuss your “inside in and outside out” requirements: what the package must retain and what it must prevent from entering.

Explore the protection topics:

  • Oxygen Protection
  • Moisture Protection
  • Light Protection
  • Flavor and Aroma Retention
  • Grease and Oil Resistance
  • Puncture and Handling Strength
  • Contamination Protection
  • Product Shelf Life

We also consider how the product will be stored and distributed:

  • Ambient or Room Temperature
  • Refrigerated
  • Frozen
  • Retail Shelf
  • Mail Order or e-Commerce
  • Multiple Storage Conditions

More barrier is not automatically better. The appropriate protection must fit the product, expected shelf life, filling process, storage environment, distribution system and project cost.

Once those requirements are understood, we can begin comparing flexible or rigid packaging structures capable of providing that protection.

  • Continue to Packaging Structures & Dielines
  • Return to Packaging Development

title: Packaging Structures & Dielines
html:
Now we can begin discussing the physical package.

The best structure is not selected only because it looks attractive. It must fit the product, barrier requirements, filling process, package size, customer use, distribution system and manufacturing quantity.

Explore packaging structures through individual images and short pop-up explanations:

  • Stand-Up Pouch
  • Stand-Up Zipper Pouch
  • Side-Gusset Bag
  • Side-Gusset Foil and Paper Bag with Wire Tie
  • Quad-Seal Bag
  • Box- or Block-Bottom Bag
  • Rollstock
  • Custom Packaging Structure

Each structure can be considered in film, foil or another material combination based on the protection and function required.

After the structure and dimensions are established, the manufacturer’s specifications create the dieline. The dieline shows where the front, back, side panels, seals, folds, zipper and other production areas will appear.

Artwork should not be finalized before the correct dieline is confirmed. The dieline becomes the production map used to position the graphic design properly.

  • View Art Templates
  • Continue to Impact Design
  • Return to Barrier Requirements

title: Impact Design
html:
Your package may be your product’s only salesperson on a retail shelf or website.

The customer may see the package for only a few seconds. The design must quickly communicate what the product is, who it is for and why the customer should consider it.

Impact Design begins with more than colors and decoration. It considers how the brand, product identity and purchasing message work together on the available package panels.

Explore the design conversation:

  • Brand and Product Positioning
  • Front-Panel Communication
  • Product Name and Primary Message
  • Visual Hierarchy
  • Color and Image Direction
  • Retail-Shelf Impact
  • Online and e-Commerce Impact
  • Adapting Existing Branding
  • Package Mockups and Presentation

The design must also fit the confirmed structure and dieline. Important information cannot be placed across folds, seals, gussets, zippers or areas that may be distorted during manufacturing.

Once the visual direction is approved, the artwork must be converted into accurate, production-ready files.

  • Continue to Prepress & Printing
  • Return to Structures & Dielines

title: Prepress & Printing
html:
A strong design must still be translated into artwork that a manufacturer can print correctly.

Prepress is the bridge between creative design and manufacturing. It prepares the graphic art for the selected material, structure, printing process and production equipment.

Explore the production-art topics:

  • Production-Ready Artwork
  • Confirmed Dieline Placement
  • Color Separation
  • Image Resolution
  • Bleeds, Seals and Print Areas
  • Barcodes and Variable Information
  • Proofing and Artwork Approval
  • Artwork Version Control

The printing method must also fit the project:

  • Digital Printing
  • Flexographic Printing and Plates
  • Gravure Printing and Cylinders

Digital, flexographic and gravure printing have different quantity, tooling, color, repeat-order and cost considerations. The decision should be based on the complete project—not simply the lowest initial price.

Once the printing requirements and production files are confirmed, the project can move into manufacturer selection and production planning.

  • Compare Printing Methods
  • Continue to Sourcing & Manufacturing
  • Return to Impact Design

title: Sourcing & Manufacturing
html:
The manufacturer must be able to produce the package—not merely quote it.

We compare manufacturing capabilities with the project’s materials, structure, printing method, quantities, quality requirements, timing and expected repeat orders.

Explore the sourcing conversation:

  • U.S. Manufacturing
  • Offshore Manufacturing
  • U.S. and Offshore Comparison
  • Manufacturer Capability
  • Minimum Production Quantities
  • Printing and Tooling Requirements
  • Samples and Production Approvals
  • Lead Times
  • Freight and Landed Cost
  • Ongoing Supply Requirements

A low unit price can become expensive if the manufacturer cannot maintain specifications, meet delivery requirements or provide consistent repeat production.

The sourcing decision should account for the complete cost and responsibility of getting approved packaging from the factory to the location where it will be filled, stored or distributed.

Before manufacturing begins, the specifications, artwork, materials, dimensions and functional requirements must be confirmed.

  • Continue to Manufacturing Quality Control
  • Return to Prepress & Printing

title: Manufacturing Quality Control
html:
Quality control begins before the production run—not after defective packaging arrives.

The manufacturer must receive and confirm the same approved specifications used throughout package development. Materials, dimensions, printing, colors, closures and functional requirements must be clearly identified.

Explore the quality-control points:

  • Approved Material and Barrier Specifications
  • Package Dimensions and Structure
  • Correct Artwork Version
  • Printing and Color Requirements
  • Zippers, Wire Ties and Closures
  • Seals and Functional Performance
  • Production Samples
  • Inspection and Approval Procedures
  • Carton, Case and Pallet Requirements
  • Final Shipment Confirmation

Quality control does not mean promising that a problem can never occur. It means establishing clear specifications, review points and production confirmations that reduce avoidable errors and help identify problems before the shipment is released.

When production is completed, the next responsibility is moving, receiving and supplying the packaging in time for the product launch.

  • Continue to Delivery, Fulfillment & Launch
  • Return to Sourcing & Manufacturing

title: Delivery, Fulfillment & Launch
html:
Packaging is not ready for use simply because manufacturing is finished.

It must leave the factory, arrive at the correct destination, be received and inspected, and remain available when the product is ready to be filled and launched.

Explore the supply conversation:

  • U.S. Factory Delivery
  • Offshore Factory Delivery
  • Ocean Freight
  • Air Freight
  • Receiving and Shipment Inspection
  • Warehousing
  • Scheduled Inventory Releases
  • Delivery to a Packer or Co-Packer
  • Initial Launch Quantity
  • Reorder Quantity and Timing
  • Ongoing Packaging Supply

Imported packaging requires additional planning for manufacturing lead time, freight, receiving and inventory. Domestic production may shorten parts of the supply chain but still requires coordination with filling and launch schedules.

The objective is not simply to receive one order. It is to establish a packaging supply process capable of supporting the initial launch and future reorders.

If the product will also be introduced online, the physical package must now be presented accurately on the website.

  • Continue to Website Product Launch
  • Return to Manufacturing Quality Control

title: Website Product Launch
html:
A package designed to sell on a shelf must also communicate clearly on a screen.

Online customers cannot pick up the package, examine it or ask a salesperson to explain it. The website must use the package design, images and product information to help replace that physical experience.

Explore the website-launch topics:

  • Package and Product Photography
  • Front, Back and Side Package Views
  • e-Commerce Product Images
  • Product Description and Benefits
  • Size and Quantity Information
  • Package Features and Reclosure
  • Consistent Branding and Colors
  • Online Retailer Requirements
  • Website Product Page
  • Launch Readiness

The package artwork and website presentation should tell the same product story. Colors, product names, sizes and primary claims should remain consistent from the manufactured package to the online listing.

Website support is optional. It becomes part of the packaging project when the product’s online presentation is necessary for a coordinated marketplace launch.

  • Continue to E-Marketing Launch
  • Return to Delivery, Fulfillment & Launch

title: E-Marketing Launch
html:
The product is packaged and ready. Now the marketplace must know it exists.

E-Marketing connects the package, product message and launch materials across the online places where customers, distributors and retailers may encounter the new product.

Explore the launch topics:

  • Social-Media Launch Images
  • New-Product Announcements
  • Email Marketing
  • Online Advertising
  • Retailer and Distributor Presentation
  • Digital Sales Materials
  • Product Demonstration Content
  • Package Images for Multiple Platforms
  • Launch Promotion
  • Continuing Product Visibility

The marketing presentation should remain consistent with the physical package and website. Customers should recognize the same product, design and message wherever they see it.

E-Marketing support is included only when it is needed. The packaging project may end with manufacturing and supply, or it may continue through a coordinated website and digital-market launch.

You do not need every answer before beginning. The Project Review gathers the available information and helps determine which packaging services are relevant.

  • Begin a Project Review
  • Contact Us With a General Packaging Question

title: Food and Beverage
html:
Food and Beverage Packaging begins with a deceptively simple question: what must the customer receive when the package is opened?

The answer may involve freshness, flavor, texture, aroma, portion size, convenience, food safety or a combination of them. We also need to understand whether the product is dry, liquid, oily, acidic, refrigerated, frozen or shelf stable, because those conditions influence the material, barrier, seals, structure and filling process.

Product and marketplace points

  • What is the product, and is it ready for commercial packaging?
  • Who is the expected customer: consumer, retailer, distributor, food-service operator or another business?
  • Will it be sold through wholesale distribution, retail shelves, online e-commerce or all of the above?
  • What package sizes are already familiar in the marketplace?
  • Will the product be filled by the owner, a co-packer or the packaging manufacturer?
  • Does the product require ambient, refrigerated or frozen distribution?

Protection and function points

  • Moisture, oxygen, light, aroma, grease or flavor protection
  • Expected unopened and opened shelf life
  • Single-use, resealable or portion-control use
  • Seal strength, leak resistance and handling durability
  • Food-contact material and manufacturer documentation
  • Retail display, storage and shipping conditions

We do not choose the package by appearance alone. We match the product and sales channel to the required protection and function, then compare structures that can be filled, sealed, printed, shipped and reordered reliably.

The next discussion may involve flexible or rigid packaging, trial and retail sizes, stand-up or gusseted structures, closures, labeling, impact design and production quantities.

  • Explore Product Protection & Barrier Requirements
  • Explore Packaging Structures & Dielines
  • Start a Food & Beverage Project Review
  • Contact Us With a General Question

title: Coffee and Tea
html:
Coffee and Tea are purchased partly by aroma, flavor and freshness—qualities the customer cannot fully inspect before opening the package.

That places unusual responsibility on the package. It must protect the product while the design communicates roast, origin, blend, flavor, format, quantity and brand position clearly enough to earn the first purchase.

Product and marketplace points

  • Whole bean, ground coffee, pods, loose tea, tea bags or another format
  • Retail, wholesale, food-service, subscription or e-commerce sales
  • Trial, common retail and bulk sizes
  • Freshly roasted product and degassing requirements
  • Premium, everyday, private-label or specialty positioning
  • Existing packaging used by direct competitors

Protection and function points

  • Oxygen, moisture, light and aroma protection
  • One-way degassing valve when the product and timing require it
  • Zipper, wire tie or another reclosure system
  • Film, foil or other barrier construction
  • Seal integrity after filling
  • Shelf stability through warehousing and distribution

A foil coffee bag is not automatically the right answer, and a valve is not automatically required for every product. We look at roast timing, filling timing, distribution, expected shelf life, customer use and quantity before establishing the specification.

Once the structure is selected, the dieline and graphic design must make roast, flavor, size and brand easy to understand on the shelf and online.

  • Compare Coffee and Tea Packaging Structures
  • Explore Barrier Requirements
  • Explore Impact Design
  • Start a Coffee or Tea Project Review

title: Bakery and Snacks
html:
Bakery and Snack Products often look simple to package until texture, breakage, grease, crumbs, portion size and shelf life enter the discussion.

A crisp product must remain crisp. A soft product must not dry out. A fragile product must survive filling, case packing, shipment and shelf handling. The package must also open and close in a way that fits how the customer actually eats the product.

Product and customer points

  • Cookies, crackers, chips, baked snacks, mixes or another product
  • Crisp, soft, fragile, oily, powdered or coated product characteristics
  • Single serving, family size, trial size or food-service quantity
  • Retail shelf, club, wholesale, vending or e-commerce sales
  • Immediate consumption or repeated opening and closing
  • Product visibility through a window or full barrier protection

Package decision points

  • Moisture and oxygen control
  • Grease resistance and seal-area cleanliness
  • Puncture and impact resistance
  • Headspace and package dimensions
  • Zipper or single-use opening
  • Stand-up pouch, side-gusset bag, rollstock, tray, carton or combined structure

The best package balances protection with the product experience. Too little protection shortens shelf life; too much empty space, material or structure can add cost without improving the product.

We define the product and channel first, test the size and function, then develop artwork on the correct dieline for the chosen structure.

  • Explore Package Size & Product Use
  • Compare Structures & Dielines
  • Start a Bakery or Snack Project Review
  • Review an Existing Package

title: Confections and Candy
html:
Confections and Candy sell through anticipation. Color, flavor, texture, gifting, indulgence and portion all influence the purchase before the package is opened.

The package must protect the product from heat, moisture, oxygen, scuffing, breakage or flavor loss while giving the design enough room to make the product immediately desirable.

Product and market points

  • Chocolate, hard candy, gummies, coated products, caramels or specialty confections
  • Individual, share, gift, seasonal, trial or bulk sizes
  • Retail shelf, counter display, gift shop, online or wholesale channels
  • Temperature and seasonal shipping exposure
  • Product contact with film, tray, wrapper, carton or inner bag
  • Premium, novelty, everyday or private-label position

Protection and presentation points

  • Moisture, oxygen, light and aroma requirements
  • Heat sensitivity and distribution conditions
  • Grease, oil or product-transfer resistance
  • Product separation, inner wrapping or trays
  • Tamper evidence and resealability
  • High-impact color, finish, window and print effects

Confectionery packaging must make the product tempting without allowing presentation to outrun performance. A beautiful carton cannot correct an inner package that does not protect the product, and a strong barrier package will not sell if the customer cannot quickly understand what is inside.

We coordinate product protection, structure and design as one project, then prepare the files and manufacturing specifications together.

  • Explore Product Protection
  • Explore Impact Design
  • Compare U.S. and Offshore Manufacturing
  • Start a Confections Project Review

title: Pet Food and Treats
html:
The pet owner makes the purchase, but the package must protect a product intended for the pet.

That means the conversation includes product ingredients and characteristics, odor and flavor retention, grease resistance, feeding quantity, repeated use, storage and the confidence the owner receives from the package.

Product and marketplace points

  • Dry food, treats, chews, supplements, toppers or another pet product
  • Dog, cat or other animal market
  • Trial, retail, multi-use and bulk sizes
  • Specialty retail, mass retail, veterinary, direct-to-consumer or e-commerce sales
  • Premium, natural, functional, training or everyday positioning
  • Package expectations established by competing products

Protection and use points

  • Moisture, oxygen, aroma and grease protection
  • Seal strength and puncture resistance
  • Zipper or other reliable reclosure
  • Stable base and convenient pouring or product access
  • Handling through retail and parcel delivery
  • Artwork, feeding information and required product information

The structure must remain functional through repeated openings, while the design helps the owner understand the product, size and intended benefit. Large packages may need different material strength, carrying and closure decisions than small treat packages.

Once the product and use pattern are clear, we can compare pouch, gusseted, quad-seal, box-bottom or other structures and develop the corresponding dieline.

  • Compare Pet Packaging Structures
  • Explore Barrier & Functional Requirements
  • Start a Pet Product Project Review
  • Review an Existing Pet Package

title: Vitamins and Supplements
html:
Vitamins and Supplements require the package to communicate confidence while protecting products that may be sensitive to moisture, oxygen, light or repeated exposure after opening.

The package must fit the dosage form, quantity, use period, distribution channel and applicable labeling responsibilities. Packaging development supports that process, but it does not replace the product owner’s regulatory or scientific review.

Product and market points

  • Capsules, tablets, powders, gummies, liquids, packets or another format
  • Daily use, trial, travel, subscription or bulk quantity
  • Retail, practitioner, fitness, direct-to-consumer or e-commerce channel
  • Existing label content and responsible regulatory review
  • Tamper-evident and child-resistant needs when applicable
  • Premium, clinical, lifestyle or value positioning

Protection and function points

  • Moisture, oxygen and light exposure
  • Product stability after repeated opening
  • Desiccant, induction seal or another supporting component when required
  • Resealability and dispensing convenience
  • Package-product compatibility
  • Lot, expiration and variable-information areas

We separate three questions: what the product requires for protection, what the customer requires for use, and what information the responsible company must present. Those answers guide the structure, closure, material and artwork layout.

When label claims or regulated statements are involved, the product owner or qualified adviser supplies the approved content. We place approved information accurately on the production dieline and prepare it for print.

  • Explore Protection & Function
  • Explore Dielines, Artwork & Prepress
  • Start a Vitamins or Supplements Project Review
  • Contact Us With a General Question

title: Health and Beauty
html:
Health and Beauty Packaging often carries two responsibilities at once: it must protect and dispense the product correctly, and it must create a visual experience consistent with the brand.

A lotion, powder, wipe, cosmetic, personal-care product or grooming item may require very different compatibility, barrier, closure and decoration decisions. We begin with the product form and how the customer will use it.

Product and customer points

  • Liquid, cream, gel, powder, wipe, solid or another product form
  • Single-use, daily-use, refill or professional application
  • Retail, salon, spa, medical-adjacent, direct-to-consumer or e-commerce sales
  • Trial, travel, retail and professional sizes
  • Product dispensing and closure expectations
  • Premium, natural, clinical, fashion or value positioning

Package decision points

  • Material compatibility with the product
  • Moisture, oxygen, light, aroma or leakage protection
  • Pumps, caps, zippers, seals, applicators or other functions
  • Tamper evidence when applicable
  • Surface, finish, color and decoration
  • Parcel-shipping durability and leak prevention

The visual design cannot be separated from the package experience. A premium appearance loses value if the closure leaks, the product is difficult to dispense or the decoration scuffs in distribution.

We coordinate function, compatibility, structure, graphics and manufacturing so the package supports the product from first impression through final use.

  • Explore Packaging Function
  • Explore Impact Design
  • Explore Sourcing & Manufacturing
  • Start a Health and Beauty Project Review

title: Household Products
html:
Household-Product Packaging must communicate purpose quickly and remain dependable during storage, transport and use.

The product may be a powder, tablet, liquid, concentrate, refill, wipe or accessory. Each form creates different questions about material compatibility, moisture, leakage, puncture, closure, dispensing and safe handling.

Product and market points

  • Cleaning, laundry, storage, maintenance, fragrance or another household use
  • Liquid, powder, solid, wipe, concentrate or refill format
  • Consumer retail, commercial, wholesale or e-commerce channel
  • Single-use, refill, repeated-use or bulk quantity
  • Storage in a cabinet, garage, vehicle, warehouse or other environment
  • Existing marketplace package and customer expectations

Protection and function points

  • Product-package compatibility
  • Leak, puncture, moisture and vapor control
  • Child-resistant or tamper-evident features when applicable
  • Pouring, dispensing, measuring or resealing
  • Clear instructions and warning-information areas supplied by the responsible company
  • Shipping case, parcel and warehouse durability

The right structure must perform through the full distribution and use cycle. A refill pouch, for example, may reduce material and shipping volume but still must pour, seal, survive drops and communicate use clearly.

We define those practical conditions before comparing materials, structures, printing methods and manufacturers.

  • Explore Functional Requirements
  • Compare Structures & Dielines
  • Start a Household Product Project Review
  • Review a Packaging Problem

title: Other Product Category
html:
Your Product Does Not Have To Fit one of our listed industries before we can begin a useful packaging conversation.

New products, specialty applications and products that cross several industries are often the reason a structured development process matters most. We begin with what the product is, what it must do and how it will reach the customer.

Starting points

  • Describe the product form, ingredients or physical characteristics relevant to packaging
  • Identify the customer and expected use
  • Identify wholesale, retail, e-commerce or mixed sales channels
  • Describe storage, handling and distribution conditions
  • Show packaging used by comparable products, if any
  • Explain what is new, unusual or unresolved about the application

Packaging questions we will develop

  • Product protection and expected shelf life
  • Package size, opening, closure and repeated use
  • Flexible, rigid or combined structure
  • Dieline, artwork and required information
  • Printing, manufacturing quantity and sourcing
  • Quality control, shipping, receiving and launch

We do not need to force the product into a familiar category. The same market-backward process still applies: product and customer first, then protection and function, then structure and design, and finally manufacturing, supply and launch.

If some technical answers are not yet known, the Project Review can identify what must be tested, confirmed or supplied by another qualified specialist before packaging is finalized.

  • Begin an Other Product Category Review
  • Explore Packaging Development
  • Contact Us With a General Packaging Question

title: Packaging Starts Here
html:
Every Packaging Project has a Different Starting Point.

You may have a product idea without a package, an existing package that needs improvement, a design ready for production, a supply problem or a failure that must be understood before another order is placed.

Where is your project today?

  • New Product – New Package
  • Existing Package Review
  • Package Redesign
  • Sourcing & Manufacturing
  • Packaging Problem or Failure
  • Cost, Supply or Quality

Choosing the project type does not assume the answer. It allows us to begin with the condition that brought you here, identify what is already known, and avoid restarting work that has already been completed correctly.

  • Contact Us With a General Question

title: Have Product – No Packaging
html:
“I have a product idea, but no package.”

That is a good place to begin because the package has not yet been limited by a premature material, structure or manufacturer decision.

We start with the product, customer and marketplace. We then work through protection, size, use, structure, design, manufacturing and supply in the order the decisions depend on one another.

What we need to understand first

  • What is the product, and how developed is it?
  • Who is expected to buy or use it?
  • Will it be sold through wholesale distribution, retail shelves, online e-commerce or all of the above?
  • What packages are customers already seeing in the marketplace?
  • How will the product be stored, filled, shipped and used?
  • What launch quantity and timing are being considered?

How the project develops

  • Product protection and functional requirements
  • Trial, retail and bulk package sizes
  • Closure, dispensing and repeated-use decisions
  • Flexible or rigid packaging structure
  • Manufacturer dieline and impact design
  • Production-ready artwork, prepress and printing
  • U.S. or offshore manufacturing
  • Quality control, shipping, receiving, supply and launch

You do not need to arrive with every answer. The development process separates decisions that can be made now from specifications that require samples, testing, manufacturer input or product-owner approval.

The objective is a package that can be manufactured and supplied—not simply a concept image that looks finished.

  • Explore Packaging Development
  • Start a New Product Project Review
  • See What to Prepare

title: Have Packaging and Product
html:
An Existing Package Gives Us Something Valuable: Real Market Experience.

Customers, production employees, packers, warehouses, retailers and shipping carriers may already have shown what works and what does not. We begin by separating visual preferences from measurable performance, supply and cost issues.

Review points

  • Product protection and actual shelf-life performance
  • Package size, empty space and customer use
  • Opening, closure, dispensing and resealability
  • Material, structure, seals and manufacturing consistency
  • Graphic impact on shelf and online
  • Filling, case packing, warehousing and shipping
  • Unit price, tooling, order quantity, freight and inventory
  • Complaints, returns, damage or recurring quality concerns

Helpful comparisons

  • Current package photographs and physical samples
  • Current specifications, dielines and artwork
  • Manufacturer quotes and recent invoices
  • Competitor packages and customer feedback
  • Damage, leakage, seal or print-failure photographs
  • Sales channels and planned product changes

The answer may be to keep the current structure and improve one feature. It may be to revise the specification, artwork, manufacturer or supply plan. A review prevents a redesign from changing parts of the package that are already serving the product well.

  • Upload Current Package Files
  • Explore Package Redesign

title: Redesign Maintaining Brand
html:
A Redesign Should Have a Reason Beyond Making the Package Simply Look New.

Perhaps the brand has changed, the product is moving into retail, the package does not communicate clearly online, a new size is needed, or the current structure no longer fits the customer’s use. We define the reason before changing familiar elements.

What may need to change

  • Brand and product positioning
  • Front-panel message and visual hierarchy
  • Package size or product quantity
  • Structure, closure or functional features
  • Barrier or material specification
  • Dieline and panel organization
  • Printing process, finishes or number of colors
  • Manufacturer, production quantity or supply plan

What may need to remain recognizable

  • Product name and established brand assets
  • Colors or visual cues customers already identify
  • Required information and approved claims
  • Package dimensions tied to filling or shelf space
  • Functional features customers value
  • Existing inventory transition requirements

We compare the current package with the intended future package and identify what the redesign must accomplish. The work then moves from approved direction to the correct dieline, production-ready artwork, proofing and controlled transition into manufacturing.

  • Explore Impact Design
  • Start a Package Redesign Review
  • Upload Current Artwork and Dielines

title: Sourcing and Manufacturing
html:
Finding a Source for Manufacturer is not the same as finding a factory that can reliably produce your package.

The sourcing conversation begins with a usable specification: material, structure, dimensions, printing, closures, quantity, quality requirements, delivery location and expected reorders. Without that information, quotations may look comparable while pricing different packages.

Sourcing points

  • U.S., offshore or comparative sourcing
  • Manufacturer equipment and actual capability
  • Minimum order and economic production quantity
  • Digital, flexographic or gravure printing
  • Plates, cylinders and other tooling
  • Samples, proofs and production approvals
  • Manufacturing and transit lead times
  • Freight, duty, brokerage and landed cost when applicable
  • Communication, corrective action and repeat-order consistency

Manufacturing points

  • Final specification and approved artwork version
  • Material and barrier confirmation
  • Dimensions, seals, zipper and functional tolerances
  • Color targets and print expectations
  • Case, pallet and shipment requirements
  • Inspection points and release approval
  • Delivery, receiving and supply schedule

The goal is not the lowest quotation on paper, film or foil. It is the best workable combination of capability, total cost, quality, timing, communication and continuing supply for this project.

  • Compare U.S. and Offshore Capabilities
  • Start a Sourcing & Manufacturing Review
  • Upload Specifications for Quotations

title: Packaging Problems or Issues
html:
When Packaging Fails, the visible damage is not always the original cause.

A leaking package may involve material compatibility, contaminated seal areas, filling temperature, sealing conditions, dimensions, handling or a combination. A scuffed print, broken zipper, delamination, odor loss or short shelf life requires the same disciplined separation of symptoms from causes.

Describe what is happening

  • What changed, and when did the problem first appear?
  • Does it affect every package, one production run or only some shipments?
  • Where was the package manufactured, filled, stored and shipped?
  • Are the current material, structure, dieline and artwork specifications available?
  • Are physical samples, photographs, lot codes and production records available?
  • Has the manufacturer, filler or material supplier already responded?

Areas to review

  • Product-package compatibility and barrier
  • Film, foil, laminate or rigid-component construction
  • Seals, closures, zippers and dimensions
  • Printing, ink adhesion, scuffing and lamination
  • Filling, sealing and production conditions
  • Case packing, pallets, warehousing and freight
  • Specification changes or uncontrolled substitutions

We document the facts, preserve samples and identify the most likely stage of failure. Some matters can be addressed through specification, manufacturer or process changes; others require independent laboratory, engineering, regulatory or legal expertise. We will distinguish those needs rather than overstate what packaging consultation alone can determine.

  • Upload Failure Photographs and Records

title: Cost, Supply and Quality
html:
Cost, Supply and Quality Are Connected. Reducing one quoted unit price may increase tooling, freight, inventory, damage or shortage costs somewhere else.

We first determine which problem is actually affecting the business: the purchase price, the total delivered cost, inconsistent quality, excessive inventory, long lead time, repeated shortages or dependence on a single source.

Cost points

  • Unit price at comparable specifications and quantities
  • Plates, cylinders, dies and other tooling
  • Freight, duty, brokerage and delivery
  • Waste, defects, rework and rejected product
  • Inventory carrying and storage requirements
  • Cost of shortages, delays or emergency freight

Supply and quality points

  • Current lead time and reorder point
  • Minimum order and release quantities
  • Forecast accuracy and seasonal demand
  • Manufacturer performance and communication
  • Specification control and approved substitutions
  • Incoming inspection and corrective-action history
  • Alternative or backup source feasibility

The review should produce a practical priority. That may be a new quotation, revised specification, second source, different printing method, better quality-control procedure, improved forecast or a planned transition to another manufacturer.

title: Our Consulting Approach
html:
Good packaging consultation begins by listening before recommending.

We want to understand your product, your customer, the marketplace and the condition that brought you to us. A startup developing its first package does not need the same opening conversation as an established company facing a seal failure, artwork transition or offshore supply problem.

Packaging decisions from the market backward

Our normal decision path is:

  • Product, customer and competitive marketplace
  • Wholesale, retail, e-commerce or combined sales channels
  • Storage, distribution and customer use
  • Product protection, barrier and functional requirements
  • Package size, structure, closure and material
  • Dieline, impact design and production-ready artwork
  • Prepress, printing and tooling
  • Sourcing, manufacturing and quality control
  • Shipping, receiving, continuing supply and launch

How the conversation works

  • We introduce one issue at a time instead of presenting an overwhelming technical questionnaire.
  • We explain why a decision matters before asking the client to choose.
  • We separate known facts from items that still require testing, samples or specialist review.
  • We preserve useful existing work rather than automatically starting over.
  • We compare total project consequences, not only the first quoted unit price.
  • We document decisions so artwork, specifications and manufacturing remain aligned.

The project may use every stage of the process or only one.

Consultation should expand only as the work requires. A client needing an existing-package review may not need a complete brand redesign; a client with approved artwork may need only prepress, manufacturing and quality-control support.

Our role is to help define the correct next decision and keep that decision connected to what comes before and after it.

title: Our President and CEO
html:
I’m Jay L. Cramblit, President and CEO of Packaging Consultants USA.

My role is to lead the client conversation and keep packaging decisions connected from the marketplace through manufacturing, supply and launch.

I do not approach a project as a catalog salesperson trying to fit every product into whatever package happens to be available.

A business owner’s view of packaging

My background includes more than 29 years of packaging experience involving distribution, package development, import management, offshore production and U.S. packaging-company operations.

Earlier business experience also shaped the way I look at packaging. I operated a gourmet cookie business in Miami and experienced the disruption that followed Hurricane Andrew.

That experience made supply, production continuity, timing and the practical consequences of interrupted operations more than abstract business terms.

Earlier in my career, I also worked in the securities industry as an Investment Banker/Stockbroker licensed as a Series 7, 24, 27 and 4 registrations. That financial and supervisory background contributes to the way I compare cost, risk, working capital, inventory and business consequences, although Packaging Consultants USA does not provide investment advice.

What I bring to the client conversation

  • Direct discussion with a lead consultant
  • Experience connecting design decisions with production realities
  • U.S. and offshore sourcing perspective
  • Understanding of quantities, tooling, freight, inventory and supply
  • A willingness to identify what is not yet known
  • Coordination with specialized resources when the project requires them

The purpose of sharing this background is not to turn the page into a resume. It is to help you understand the perspective behind the consultation: packaging must protect and present the product, but it must also be manufacturable, financeable, deliverable and available when the business needs it.

title: Packaging Experience
html:
Packaging experience becomes useful when it helps answer the next practical question in your project.

The question may be whether a film or foil structure can provide the required barrier, whether a zipper belongs in the seal area, whether digital printing fits the quantity, whether an offshore quotation includes the full delivered cost, or whether a recurring defect begins with the specification or the manufacturing process.

Areas of packaging experience

  • Flexible packaging distribution and development
  • Film and foil barrier structures
  • Stand-up, side-gusset, quad-seal and box- or block-bottom packages
  • Package dimensions, closures and functional requirements
  • Manufacturer dielines and artwork coordination
  • Graphic development, prepress and production readiness
  • Digital, flexographic and gravure printing considerations
  • Plates, cylinders and production tooling
  • U.S. and offshore sourcing and import management
  • Manufacturing approvals and quality-control coordination
  • Shipping, receiving, inventory and continuing supply
  • Packaging problems, specification reviews and corrective direction

How experience is applied

We do not begin by placing every capability in front of the client. We introduce the experience relevant to the present decision.

If the product has no package, we begin with market and protection. If the artwork does not fit the structure, we begin with the correct dieline. If a shipment failed, we begin with facts, samples and records. If the price appears high, we compare equivalent specifications, quantities, tooling, freight, quality and inventory.

No consultant should claim to replace every technical discipline.

Food science, product formulation, regulatory approval, laboratory testing, engineering, legal review and specialized logistics may require qualified professionals in those fields. Packaging consultation helps identify and coordinate those needs while maintaining the packaging-development path.

title: U.S. / Offshore Capabilities
html:
Should this package be manufactured in the United States or offshore?

There is no responsible one-word answer. The correct comparison depends on specification, quantity, tooling, print quality, lead time, freight, working inventory, communication, quality control and the cost of interruption.

U.S. manufacturing considerations

  • Potentially shorter production and transit times
  • Easier shipment, communication and plant coordination
  • Lower freight complexity for some projects
  • Possible smaller economic quantities, depending on process
  • Domestic tooling and printing capabilities
  • Faster response when specifications or demand change

Offshore manufacturing considerations

  • Access to particular equipment, structures or high-volume economics
  • Longer production, ocean transit and customs timelines
  • Freight, duty, brokerage and inland delivery
  • Larger minimums or inventory commitments in some cases
  • Time-zone, language and documentation requirements
  • Pre-shipment approval and quality-control planning

The comparison points

  • Are both manufacturers quoting the same material, barrier, dimensions and print?
  • Are plates, cylinders, dies and other tooling included?
  • What is the complete landed cost at the delivery location?
  • How much inventory and working capital does each option require?
  • What happens if the forecast changes or a shipment is delayed?
  • How will repeat-order quality be controlled?

Offshore is not automatically cheaper, and domestic is not automatically faster or better.

We compare the complete supply decision for the specific project.

A first production run may favor one source while mature repeat volume favors another. Some clients may also consider a primary and secondary supply strategy when specifications, quantities and tooling permit it.
